graph.core_idea: Claude is used as an agent state machine, one session per role, every message between agents a file in a vault and every outgoing email a draft a person sends; the phases take you from one session to a scheduled team without ever breaking that rule.

nodes.label: Claude as a state machine
nodes.summary: Each role is one session that reads its state from a vault, does one kind of work, writes files back and stops; the conductor makes this literal.

nodes.label: Accounts of the agent's own
nodes.summary: A Workspace mailbox on a domain you own, a Claude Team seat, a GitHub account on the same identity; never your own inbox.

nodes.label: Connectors enabled, then connected
nodes.summary: On a Team plan the owner enables connectors for the organisation; the agent's own account then connects, so the OAuth grants live only there.

nodes.label: The inbox role
nodes.summary: The one session that reads the mailbox, labels, moves, summarises and captures what people wrote into the CRM.

nodes.label: The policy as a table
nodes.summary: Reach, mandate, gap and barriers written before the first run; most barriers in front of a single session are the policy and nothing technical, and the table says so.

nodes.label: Roles: @inbox, @drafts, @crm, @briefs, @dev
nodes.summary: Each role a session with a policy short enough to check; every account has the same reach to the mailbox, two have it in their mandate, one may write.

nodes.label: Email-FS lite
nodes.summary: A message is a file with email headers and typed blocks; mailroom, inbox, done and outbox folders; each role writes only its own folders; one commit per cycle after a leak check.

nodes.label: The agent drafts, a person sends
nodes.summary: Nothing is sent by an agent; the draft is Cc'd to the person, its hash is logged, and the inbox role records the send from the Sent folder afterwards.

nodes.label: The security hold
nodes.summary: The one exception: the security role may send one email to one address on a critical finding, and writes a hold file that stops every agent and every run until a person releases it.

nodes.label: The conductor
nodes.summary: A scheduled session that runs every role exactly once in a fixed order with a time box, leak-checks and pushes after each step, and writes a report; a security role runs first and last.

nodes.label: The clone cost
nodes.summary: Clone time grows with the number of commits, not file size; fifty commits a day made a seven-minute clone after three days. Commit once per run and compact when a clone passes five minutes.

nodes.label: A leaked write key means a new vault
nodes.summary: History keeps what was committed, so a key quoted in a committed file is fixed by a fresh vault seeded from the current files, not by a redaction; scan for other people's secret shapes too.

nodes.label: Interfaces for the moment
nodes.summary: The Now card and the waiting-on board, computed from the vault files when the page opens, nothing stored; each one gets a policy.

nodes.label: The record
nodes.summary: Every message a file, every draft in the mailbox, every decision a row: a footprint that can be read afterwards without touching anything.

nodes.label: Trust built from the record
nodes.summary: You do not have to believe what the agent says it did; you can read what it did, and give it more as the drafts you did not change pile up.

nodes.label: The agents' own account
nodes.summary: Each role describes what it reads, writes and refuses, in its own words; the dev role's paragraph and the briefs role's picture of the twelve-agent team are the first two.

quotes.text: Nothing is sent by an agent.
quotes.why: The rule that never changes, and the reason the setup gives the person more control rather than less.

quotes.text: You do not have to believe what the agent says it did. You can read what it did.
quotes.why: Why the record is the point for someone learning to trust a set of agents.

quotes.text: A leaked write key means a new vault, not an edit.
quotes.why: The lesson the record taught on day five: history keeps what was committed.

articles.title: Price it, then give it away: the early access programme as the next step after "do they miss it"
articles.teaser: Define the product, price it, deliver it at a cost that grows a step at a time, then offer it free to people who know you and measure what it costs them.

graph.teaser: Define the product, price it, deliver it at a cost that grows a step at a time, then offer it free to people who know you and measure what it costs them.
graph.core_idea: A price is a statement of what you think the thing is worth, and giving it away at that price to people who already know you is the cleanest test of whether the statement is true, provided you measure and cut what the free offer costs them.

nodes.label: Do they miss it
nodes.summary: The earlier article's test: hand the thing to people for free, briefly, then take it away, and ask whether they miss it.

nodes.label: Define the product
nodes.summary: For RiskMandate the thing somebody receives is an Agent Behaviour Policy for one agent, as an encrypted vault the customer holds the keys to, with the mandate corrected for their deployment.

nodes.label: Price it before you give it away
nodes.summary: A price is a statement of what you think the thing is worth, and giving it away at that stated price to people who know you is the cleanest test of whether the statement is true.

nodes.label: The four-tier ladder
nodes.summary: Ten pounds for the pack downloaded, fifty for a working vault, five hundred for the vault corrected for your situation, fifteen hundred for two sessions and a professional's signature.

nodes.label: Cost that grows a step at a time
nodes.summary: The agentic workflow means the marginal customer costs a little more, not a lot more, so serving the twentieth customer costs close to serving the second.

nodes.label: Offer it to the people who already know you
nodes.summary: Early adopters, power users and past customers get the first twenty, as a thank-you and as the best possible test group, because their silence means the most.

nodes.label: Free is never free for the other side
nodes.summary: Engaging costs them reading, thinking, deciding and finding a slot, so the first measurement the programme makes is of that attrition and the exercise is to reduce it.

nodes.label: Do not make them apply
nodes.summary: "We have twenty of these in the first round. Would you like one? If not, I will give it to someone else" is honest about scarcity and leaves them nothing to do but say yes or no.

nodes.label: RiskMandate early access programme
nodes.summary: Live on 30 September 2026, invite only, it gives the five-hundred-pound tier to people who already run an agent with real access and asks them to say where it is wrong.

nodes.label: The answer is brutal either way
nodes.summary: If friendlies take it and ask for more, the question becomes price; if they say it is interesting but have no time, the problem is not the price and you go back to the drawing board.

nodes.label: What we count
nodes.summary: Policies created, customised, used, and scenarios run, plus corrections received and the minutes each step cost the person on the other side.

nodes.label: For the agents running this
nodes.summary: The list, the short message with no application, the clock on every step, daily counts, every stop recorded as a product change, a stop rule set before the first message, and this article as the record.

nodes.label: The site is becoming the memory
nodes.summary: An agent picking this up in a year should read, in order, the earlier article, the published offer, this article and the vault holding the counts, so it gets context rather than instructions.

quotes.text: A price is a statement of what you think the thing is worth. Giving it away at that stated price, to people who know you, is the cleanest test of whether the statement is true.
quotes.why: The whole method in two sentences: the price is set first and the free offer is the test of it.

quotes.text: None of that is zero, and all of it is paid by them.
quotes.why: The part that is easy to leave out: the offer costs the other side attention and schedule, and that cost is what the programme measures.

articles.title: Footprint and blast radius: what the agent actually did, and what it would have cost
articles.teaser: Footprint is what an agent actually did, read afterwards from logs and vault history; blast radius is what a row of its reach would cost the business today.

graph.teaser: Footprint is what an agent actually did, read afterwards from logs and vault history; blast radius is what a row of its reach would cost the business today.
graph.core_idea: Add two words to the Agent Behaviour Policy: footprint, what the agent actually did, read afterwards from the record and compared with the mandate, and blast radius, what a row of its reach would cost the business if used in full today, with whether there is a way back.

nodes.label: Reach, mandate, gap and barriers
nodes.summary: RiskMandate's policy is written before the agent runs: reach is what it can do, mandate what you asked, gap the difference in both directions, barriers what stands in the way.

nodes.label: Only a boundary is a control
nodes.summary: A barrier is a boundary, a setting, an expectation or nothing, and most of what organisations call controls turn out to be expectations once they are typed.

nodes.label: Footprint
nodes.summary: The set of things the agent actually did, in a period, read from the record afterwards; the same kind of list as the reach and the mandate, but evidence rather than a decision.

nodes.label: Where the footprint comes from
nodes.summary: The connector's audit log, the model provider's tool-call record, a connector twin's replay, a vault's commit history, the append lanes and the agents' own messages.

nodes.label: Reading, not intercepting
nodes.summary: Nothing sits inline, a copy of the logs or a read key is enough so an outside reviewer can do it, and the footprint accumulates so some findings only exist at the twelfth week.

nodes.label: Footprint in the gap
nodes.summary: The agent did something within its reach and outside its mandate and nothing stopped it, which is a near miss, and it resolves by adding the row to the mandate or putting a boundary in front of it.

nodes.label: Dormant mandate
nodes.summary: A row the owner asked for that the footprint never shows: an over-stated mandate, a check that was relied on and never ran, or a shortfall the reach inventory missed.

nodes.label: Expected-use hint
nodes.summary: Each mandate row wants a hint of how often the owner expects to see it, always, sometimes, rarely, hopefully never, so a dormant row can be told from a contingency that was never needed.

nodes.label: The mandate as practised
nodes.summary: Read the footprint for a month and you have the rows the agent actually uses, with the near misses marked, as the first draft of a policy for an agent that has none.

nodes.label: Blast radius
nodes.summary: What it would cost the business if a row were used in full, today, defined over the reach because whoever takes the agent over inherits its reach and ignores its mandate.

nodes.label: Whether there is a way back
nodes.summary: Two rows with the same scope and different reversibility are not the same risk, and the policy should say so.

nodes.label: Same footprint, different blast radius
nodes.summary: An agent drops a staging table three times over two months; the row is identical each time, and only on day forty-one, when it held six weeks of real records, is it the incident.

nodes.label: What the cloud already does
nodes.summary: AWS, Google Cloud and Microsoft Entra already compare permissions granted with permissions used, but a permission set carries no statement of intent, so there is no dormant mandate.

nodes.label: A vault is a footprint recorder by construction
nodes.summary: Every commit is signed, versioned and append-only, so an agent working in a vault leaves a footprint whether or not anyone intended to collect one, and most of what sgit does shrinks the irreversible part of the blast radius.

nodes.label: The gap plus blast radius is the risk
nodes.summary: The gap is exposure, blast radius is impact, and the person who accepts a gap is accepting its blast radius, which until now the policy did not state.

nodes.label: Reading our own footprint
nodes.summary: Ten agents, six with a written policy, eight days of commit history; the footprint against the six policies is still to be read and published as the second article.

quotes.text: The mandate tells you what you hoped for. The reach tells you what you are exposed to.
quotes.why: Why blast radius is defined over the reach, not the mandate: an attacker inherits the reach.

quotes.text: The footprint is how you get near misses for agents without waiting for the luck to run out.
quotes.why: The payoff of reading the footprint against the gap: incidents and near misses are the same events with different luck.

articles.title: Custom UIs are not the exception: the inbox in 2026, where every message has its own universe
articles.teaser: Every message has a graph, so it can be shaped for the reader's moment; a custom interface per moment is now how interfaces get made, and each gets a policy.

graph.teaser: Every message has a graph, so it can be shaped for the reader's moment; a custom interface per moment is now how interfaces get made, and each gets a policy.
graph.core_idea: Every message has a graph with altitudes, so a message is designed for the recipient's moment rather than the sender's thread; a custom interface per moment is how interfaces now get made, each one commoditising the next, and each is an agent surface that gets a policy.

nodes.label: The follow-up problem
nodes.summary: Following up is harder than doing the work, because every person has a different context and the thread you share hides its own structure.

nodes.label: Every message has a graph
nodes.summary: Extract the actions, questions, statements, decisions and concepts from every message and a thread stops being a thread and becomes a graph.

nodes.label: Altitudes
nodes.summary: There is a graph for the block inside a message, the message, the conversation, the company and the contact, each navigable on its own and pointing up and down.

nodes.label: Email is a medium
nodes.summary: The design brief for a message is the recipient's moment when they open it, not the sender's thread, so send what they need in the shape they need it.

nodes.label: A message is a projection
nodes.summary: A message to a person is a projection of the conversation graph, for one reader, at the moment they open it, and a thread is only the raw stream.

nodes.label: Genesis, custom, product, commodity
nodes.summary: Everything moves from genesis through custom-built to product to commodity, and every new interface built is a thing commoditised for next time.

nodes.label: Custom interfaces are not the exception
nodes.summary: A custom interface per message, per thread, per topic, per question is not an exception; it is how interfaces get made.

nodes.label: The page that is both the to-do and the place to act
nodes.summary: A page lists the PDFs still owed and gives a place to drop them, through the vault's append lane, with no context switch, no second tool and no email.

nodes.label: Append lane
nodes.summary: A write-only channel anyone with the token can drop a file into, which the vault's owner drains and processes in order.

nodes.label: Email-FS blocks
nodes.summary: The fenced decision, answer and status blocks that Email-FS-lite uses so agents can read each other's asks without parsing prose, rendered as an interface for a human.

nodes.label: Eight days, not one afternoon
nodes.summary: From 25 September to 2 October 2026 a small team of agents and one human went from an empty vault to a working way of doing outreach, with sixteen CRM interface releases and around 230 commits.

nodes.label: Every tap teaches the next interface
nodes.summary: A moment gets a shape, the shape gets a decision, the decision is written to the vault as a record, and the record shapes the next version of the interface.

nodes.label: Why it compounds
nodes.summary: Every interface makes the next one better, each one teaches the agent how its user wants to work, and when automation outgrows the inbox the interface becomes the prioritisation.

nodes.label: The future of email
nodes.summary: The future of email is sender-served structure, read by the recipient's agent, with the inbox as one view of the graph, and a plain email still works on day one.

nodes.label: Ten agents and one human
nodes.summary: Ten agents with narrow jobs and one human who decides, talking to each other in files, each writing only its own folders, six with a written Agent Behaviour Policy.

nodes.label: An interface is an agent surface, so it gets a policy
nodes.summary: A page that drops files into a vault, answers questions or lets a model read a CRM has a grant, a mandate, a delta and barriers, so it gets a policy like any agent.

quotes.text: Every time I ask an agent in chat for something a page could have shown me, that is the next interface.
quotes.why: The measurable version of the title: the trigger that produces each custom interface.

quotes.text: The graph is the medium. Email, cards, voice and boards are views of it.
quotes.why: The turn where email stops being the medium and becomes one projection of the graph.

articles.title: The ultimate insider: agents, the infrastructure that cannot hold them, and risk management that cannot keep up
articles.teaser: Agents, the infrastructure meant to contain them, and risk management run on spreadsheets are arriving at once, and together they are one scenario.

graph.teaser: Agents, the infrastructure meant to contain them, and risk management run on spreadsheets are arriving at once, and together they are one scenario.
graph.core_idea: Agents are the insider threat that never scaled before, the infrastructure was designed for none of it, and risk management runs at the speed of spreadsheets, so the way out is to constrain the agent in order to trust it.

nodes.label: A threat is anything that causes business impact
nodes.summary: A threat does not need to be malicious, and most of the worst damage was a bug, a misconfiguration or a person doing something that was allowed and should not have been.

nodes.label: The insider threat never scaled
nodes.summary: There were two kinds of insider, a human bounded by hours and conscience and static code that did what it was written to do, and both were constrained by something soft but real.

nodes.label: An agent is a reasoning engine in a loop
nodes.summary: An agent is a language model in a loop with tools and an objective, and unlike any insider before it has skills: every language, every schema, the ability to write its own connectors and try again.

nodes.label: The lethal trifecta
nodes.summary: Give a model private data, untrusted content and a way to communicate outward, and it can be turned against you by a document it reads.

nodes.label: Five incidents
nodes.summary: Replit, Gemini CLI, Amazon Q, EchoLeak and the AI-orchestrated espionage campaign, of which three were not attacks but agents being agents.

nodes.label: 82 machine identities per human
nodes.summary: Agents are arriving into a population of identities that is already unmanaged, with 42 per cent of machine identities holding privileged access.

nodes.label: The infrastructure that cannot hold them
nodes.summary: Recovery, identity, permissions and containment were all built for code that stays where you put it, and the stack falls over on its own.

nodes.label: The grant and the mandate
nodes.summary: Cloud permissions are the union of everything anyone ever needed, so an agent's grant is not what you meant but everything the role accumulated.

nodes.label: The two outages
nodes.summary: A DNS race condition took down a large part of AWS US-East-1 for over fourteen hours, and a configuration file that doubled in size broke Cloudflare and much of the web.

nodes.label: Risk management at the speed of spreadsheets
nodes.summary: 48 per cent of organisations track risk in spreadsheets, reviewed quarterly, when the decisions now have to be made in seconds and in advance.

nodes.label: The chain to pulling the plug
nodes.summary: Because the register cannot see what the agent can reach it cannot say what the risk is, cannot decide whether it fits the appetite, cannot fund the controls, and the plug comes out.

nodes.label: Nobody has to report
nodes.summary: Companies are not required to disclose most of what agents do to them, and aviation solved this fifty years ago with confidential reporting that cyber has nothing like.

nodes.label: The collision
nodes.summary: An entity inside the company with reach we have not measured, controls we cannot rely on, and a decision process too slow to matter before, during or after the incident.

nodes.label: Agent Behaviour Policy
nodes.summary: Grant measured, mandate elicited, delta derived, barrier recorded, with each barrier typed honestly as a boundary, a setting, an expectation or nothing.

nodes.label: Contain in layers
nodes.summary: Identity per agent, twins that journal every call, network segmentation, and append-only records in vaults the host cannot read.

nodes.label: Brakes are what let a car go fast
nodes.summary: The more you can constrain an agent, the more you can trust it, and the more autonomy you can afford to give it.

quotes.text: Three of those five were not attacks. They were agents being agents.
quotes.why: The distance between benign and malicious agent damage is a prompt, which is why the insider framing fits.

quotes.text: The more you can constrain an agent, the more you can trust it, and the more autonomy you can afford to give it.
quotes.why: The irony the talk would end on, and the turn from the problem to the way out.

articles.title: The reader was always the product: a corrected history of how news got into this mess
articles.teaser: News has sold the reader to advertisers since 1833; the web took the monopoly, the platforms made the reader measurable, and AI took the traffic.

graph.teaser: News has sold the reader to advertisers since 1833; the web took the monopoly, the platforms made the reader measurable, and AI took the traffic.
graph.core_idea: The reader has been the product since 1833 and the money has always flowed to whoever owned the road, so the fix is to stop charging for the road and charge for the cargo: the story as a graph with every claim tied to hashed evidence.

nodes.label: The reader was always the product
nodes.summary: The reader stopped being the customer in 1833 and became the audience sold to the advertiser, and by 2005 advertising was 82% of American newspaper revenue.

nodes.label: Penny press
nodes.summary: The New York Sun of September 1833 sold on the street for a cent and was paid for by advertising while other papers relied on high-priced subscriptions.

nodes.label: Unregulated toll bridge
nodes.summary: A monopoly city newspaper was the only way for a local advertiser to reach local households, and its margins of 20 to 30 per cent paid for the reporting.

nodes.label: Classifieds collapse
nodes.summary: Classifieds were about 40% of revenue and fell from $19.6 billion in 2000 to about $6 billion in 2009 once Craigslist let people list a sofa for free.

nodes.label: The measurable reader
nodes.summary: Cookies in 1996 and AdSense in 2003 let the reader be followed from page to page, and by 2017 Google and Meta took 54.7% of American digital advertising.

nodes.label: Publisher as tenant
nodes.summary: Publishers depended on traffic from companies that could switch it off, and Facebook referrals to news sites fell 58% in six years.

nodes.label: Novelty beats truth
nodes.summary: False news on Twitter was 70% more likely to be retweeted than true news, spread by humans not bots, and Facebook weighted an anger reaction at five times a like.

nodes.label: Provenance is labour
nodes.summary: Following a claim to its source is hours of a person's time, and newsrooms that lost 57% of their jobs cut those hours first because they did not move the click.

nodes.label: AI removes the traffic
nodes.summary: Search traffic to publishers fell a third in the year to November 2025 while the crawlers that replaced it fetch tens of thousands of pages per reader they send back.

nodes.label: Back to selling to readers, by rent
nodes.summary: Circulation revenue overtook advertising in 2021, but what is sold is the subscription, unlimited access priced for the reader who forgets to cancel.

nodes.label: 402 Payment Required
nodes.summary: HTTP/1.1 reserved a status code in 1997 for digital cash or micropayment systems, and it is still reserved for future use with no browser having implemented it.

nodes.label: Mental transaction costs
nodes.summary: Szabo and Shirky argued that deciding whether an article is worth two cents costs more than two cents, an argument that does not apply to an agent with a wallet.

nodes.label: Advertising as the default
nodes.summary: The banner ad, the cookie, the pop-up and AdSense were small decisions that together made advertising the default model to support online content.

nodes.label: People pay when paying is easy
nodes.summary: A million iTunes songs sold in the first week in 2003 and Substack passed five million paid subscriptions in 2025, in an industry that insisted people never would.

nodes.label: Charge for the cargo, not the road
nodes.summary: Sell the story as a graph, every claim walked to frozen and hashed evidence, in pence and on demand, with the money walking back to whoever made the fact.

quotes.text: The reader stopped being the customer in 1833. The reader became the audience that was sold to the customer, and the cover price became a way of proving the audience existed.
quotes.why: The most important of the four corrections: the web did not make the reader the product, the penny press did.

quotes.text: The fix is to stop charging for the road and start charging for the cargo.
quotes.why: The four eras end here: the money followed whoever owned distribution, so the proposal is to sell the evidence itself.

articles.title: Six agents, one inbox: what a real multi-agent setup taught me about access policies
articles.teaser: An access policy for an agent is only as real as its worst row: every rule in a real six-agent setup, graded by how it is enforced today.

graph.teaser: An access policy for an agent is only as real as its worst row: every rule in a real six-agent setup, graded by how it is enforced today.
graph.core_idea: Write an agent's access policy as a table with a column for how each rule is enforced, and the policy is exactly as strong as the row that says the agent has been told.

nodes.label: The worst row
nodes.summary: If the enforcement column says the agent has been told, that row is a hope, and the policy is exactly as strong as that hope on the day something goes wrong.

nodes.label: The account is the blast radius
nodes.summary: Every session an agent opens through a connector runs as the account that authorised it, with everything that account can reach.

nodes.label: Dedicated accounts per agent
nodes.summary: A dedicated Workspace seat, a dedicated Claude seat and a dedicated GitHub account per agent, so the worst a session can do is bounded by what its account can see.

nodes.label: Organisational unit
nodes.summary: An account of its own puts each agent in its own organisational unit, and Google Workspace applies its Gmail compliance rules per unit.

nodes.label: Restrict delivery
nodes.summary: A delivery restriction to my own domain means that even if the reader sends, it can only reach me.

nodes.label: Attachment compliance
nodes.summary: An outbound rule that strips attachments turns a policy into a property of the mail system.

nodes.label: Scope limits on third-party apps
nodes.summary: The sharpest tool in the box cannot express drafts only, because the Gmail API puts drafting and sending in the same grant.

nodes.label: Six roles
nodes.summary: The reader, the mailbox, the inbox, the CRM, the dev team and the site editor, each with a policy short enough to check and differing on who may send.

nodes.label: The exception arrived before the policy
nodes.summary: The reader that must never reply must reply when the message came from me, and never became never, unless on day one.

nodes.label: Signature registry
nodes.summary: The append-lane machinery of per-session keys and a pinned registry is what would let the reader verify a message came from me, once my key is in it.

nodes.label: The attachment finding
nodes.summary: An agent found that create_draft and update_draft accept an attachments array and proved it with a 17 KB signed PDF that arrived intact.

nodes.label: The documentation disagrees with itself
nodes.summary: One vendor page says the Gmail connector is read-only and another says it can send, reply and forward, so a policy that cites the documentation has cited a moving target.

nodes.label: Connector twin
nodes.summary: Before you write down what an agent may do, replay what it can do.

nodes.label: Enforcement ladder
nodes.summary: Identity boundaries and keys enforce themselves, compliance rules enforce at the platform, approval prompts enforce at the human, and everything else is the agent doing as it was told.

nodes.label: The policy table
nodes.summary: One rule per row across six roles, with the column that says whether it is enforced, an admin rule, an approval, or told.

nodes.label: Cowork and Claude Code reach
nodes.summary: The Cowork agent has no GitHub connector and cannot open the repository, while the Claude Code agent on the same seat edits the site.

quotes.text: An access policy for an agent is only as real as its worst row.
quotes.why: The claim the whole article is built to test, stated so it can be wrong.

quotes.text: The only way to know what a connector can do is to try.
quotes.why: The attachment finding showed a policy written from documentation was wrong.

articles.title: Sixteen thousand fetches, ten clicks, and a token bill nobody is sending: the case for paying publishers to be easy to read
articles.teaser: AI answer engines pay to read the web as HTML; a publisher who serves markdown, dates, hashes and a typed graph saves them tokens and should get a share.

graph.teaser: AI answer engines pay to read the web as HTML; a publisher who serves markdown, dates, hashes and a typed graph saves them tokens and should get a share.
graph.core_idea: The fetches that answer engines make are a token cost to the fetcher as well as a loss to the publisher, and a publisher who serves structure is saving the provider money it already spends, so a share of that saving is owed.

nodes.label: Sixteen thousand fetches, ten clicks
nodes.summary: A week of Cloudflare AI answer retrievals for baekdal.com came to 16,000 requests and the referrals they sent back came to 10.

nodes.label: The commons reading
nodes.summary: The answer engines graze on a shared field and give nothing back, so the field will be fenced and the grazing priced.

nodes.label: The second reading
nodes.summary: Those 16,000 fetches are also a cost to the fetcher, because every one is a page of HTML parsed, extracted and turned into tokens.

nodes.label: HTML against markdown
nodes.summary: On this site's 183 pages the markdown twin is 62% fewer tokens than the HTML, and Cloudflare's own example is 81%.

nodes.label: The re-fetch waste
nodes.summary: More than half of legitimate bot crawl traffic re-fetches pages that have not changed, and more than 90% of pages crawlers process are unique, which defeats the cache layer.

nodes.label: The arithmetic
nodes.summary: Sixteen thousand fetches a week of HTML is about 113 million tokens against 43 million as markdown, tens of dollars a week for one site and a line on a very large invoice across the web.

nodes.label: A markdown twin and a map
nodes.summary: Every page served as clean markdown at a predictable address, with an llms.txt at the root, generated from the same source so the two cannot drift.

nodes.label: A date and a hash
nodes.summary: Tell the fetcher when the page last changed and give it a hash, so a fetch of an unchanged page can be skipped altogether.

nodes.label: Frozen, hashed sources
nodes.summary: Claims that carry the byte range and SHA-256 of the page they came from do the verification round trip once for everyone.

nodes.label: A typed graph
nodes.summary: A fractal semantic graph lets an agent load exactly as much as the question needs, so the tokens saved are the page minus the answer.

nodes.label: Every rail prices the content
nodes.summary: Pay per crawl, RSL, the IAB's protocols, Microsoft's marketplace, Perplexity's pool and Cloudflare's pay per use all price the fetch or the citation, and none pays a site for being cheap to read.

nodes.label: The exchange
nodes.summary: A provider that spends fewer tokens reading a site that serves structure has saved money it was already spending, and should hand part of the saving back as a rebate for the format.

nodes.label: Tokens as currency
nodes.summary: A publisher could be paid in the provider's own credits, which are the budget that builds the site, and News Corp already took part of its deal in credits.

nodes.label: The broker
nodes.summary: A single site cannot send the invoice, so the broker will be whoever sits between the bots and the sites, which today means Cloudflare, TollBit and the marketplaces.

nodes.label: Baekdal wants an audience
nodes.summary: Tokens are not an audience, though structure is what makes a citation land on the right paragraph and tokens are the budget that builds the site the reader arrives at.

nodes.label: What would settle it
nodes.summary: Three numbers per domain for a week of real retrieval, the tokens spent on HTML, the tokens the twin would have cost and the fetches a change signal would have skipped, live in the providers' logs.

quotes.text: Every step exists today. What does not exist is anyone paying for them.
quotes.why: The gap the proposal is written to fill: the publisher's half of the exchange is already built.

quotes.text: It is not new money. It is money being spent today, by the answer engines, on reading the web the hard way.
quotes.why: Why a rebate on waste is the easiest money in the negotiation to agree to.

articles.title: A supply chain of vaults: how GenAI, open data and small custom tools could bring the price of food down
articles.teaser: The food chain is a data problem: one encrypted vault per party, joined by append lanes and a typed graph, could cut the waste that keeps prices high.

graph.teaser: The food chain is a data problem: one encrypted vault per party, joined by append lanes and a typed graph, could cut the waste that keeps prices high.
graph.core_idea: The food chain is logistics, logistics is a data problem, and a supply chain of encrypted vaults with small custom tools built once by GenAI could bring the price of food down, if somebody runs the experiment.

nodes.label: The food pound
nodes.summary: For a kilo of supermarket apples selling at £2.20, the grower's costs were 76p and their profit 3p.

nodes.label: A chain of spreadsheets
nodes.summary: Each hop keeps its own record of the same consignment, mostly in spreadsheets, and an order, a delivery note, a grade, a price and a payment date are typed in five times.

nodes.label: Food lost before retail
nodes.summary: The FAO puts the share of food lost between harvest and retail at 13.3% in 2023, and a good deal of it is information.

nodes.label: The chokepoint
nodes.summary: Once a buyer holds a large share of a farm's output it names the price, which is the mechanism Giblin and Doctorow call a chokepoint.

nodes.label: The limit of regulation
nodes.summary: Codes of practice regulate the conduct of the party with the systems and leave the party without them exactly where it was.

nodes.label: All of it is logistics
nodes.summary: Everything between the field and the shelf is a workflow, and logistics is a data problem before it is a transport problem.

nodes.label: A supply chain of vaults
nodes.summary: Every party in the chain holds its own encrypted, versioned vault, readable by nobody who does not hold a key, including the host.

nodes.label: Append lanes
nodes.summary: Write-only channels through which one party can put a file into another's vault without being able to read anything there.

nodes.label: One graph across the vaults
nodes.summary: Each vault keeps its own vocabulary and typed edges join them, which is what makes waste visible.

nodes.label: Use GenAI not to use GenAI
nodes.summary: The model is used once, to turn a grower's brief into a working tool, and production runs on plain files with no model in the line.

nodes.label: Villagers and town planners
nodes.summary: A small company takes the finished tool and runs it for a hundred other growers, paid because it keeps working rather than by the seat.

nodes.label: The price hypothesis
nodes.summary: The hypothesis is that a supply chain run this way brings the price of food and goods down, and the evidence is partial.

nodes.label: The deflation dogma
nodes.summary: The BIS found the link between falling goods prices and lower growth to be weak, and a cheaper loaf because the chain wasted less is not a Japanese lost decade.

nodes.label: The cost of not sharing
nodes.summary: About 80% of industrial data is never used, and every grower who learns what a buyer will reject learns it alone.

nodes.label: Open-weight models
nodes.summary: Companies that build on open weights can run a near-frontier model inside their own environment and innovate on top of it.

nodes.label: The experiment
nodes.summary: Nobody has put a grower, a packer and a buyer on vaults and run a season through them, and this article is the brief for that experiment.

quotes.text: Everything between the field and the shelf is a workflow, and every workflow is a set of records moving between parties.
quotes.why: The step that turns a food price problem into a data problem the vaults can address.

quotes.text: What we never calculate is the economic cost of not sharing.
quotes.why: The second memo's argument, that openness is the other half of the case.

articles.title: Every risk is already accepted. The only question is by whom, and for how long.
articles.teaser: A risk exists the moment the exposure does, so somebody is already carrying it; the only questions worth asking are who has accepted it and until when.

graph.teaser: A risk exists the moment the exposure does, so somebody is already carrying it; the only questions worth asking are who has accepted it and until when.
graph.core_idea: Every risk an organisation has is already accepted by somebody, so the only questions are who has accepted it and until when; a register that cannot answer them, on facts, is disconnected from reality.

nodes.label: Every risk is already accepted
nodes.summary: A risk exists the moment the exposure does, so the organisation is carrying it from the start, signed for or not.

nodes.label: There is no deny button
nodes.summary: You cannot vote a fact out of existence, and a register that lets you reject a risk lets you pretend.

nodes.label: Three doors
nodes.summary: Accept it personally for a stated interval, fund the work that reduces it, or fix it so the facts that make it true stop holding; silence is not a fourth door.

nodes.label: Unaccepted is critical
nodes.summary: A risk nobody has accepted rests on whoever is nearest and rolls upward to their boss, and then to theirs, until somebody signs.

nodes.label: The interval is the decision
nodes.summary: One hour means more data, four hours is a priority-one incident, one month is assemble and fund, and six months is do nothing and review it then, with a name on it.

nodes.label: Accepted is not acceptable
nodes.summary: Accepted is an act by a named person on a date for an interval; acceptable is a threshold, and the dangerous state is a risk over the line that nobody has signed for.

nodes.label: EU AI Act, Article 9(5)
nodes.summary: Providers of high-risk AI systems must have residual risk judged to be acceptable, and the Act never defines the word.

nodes.label: Every risk has a boss
nodes.summary: Every risk has a holder, every holder has a boss, and every path ends at the board, computed rather than reported, and nobody can accept on anybody else's behalf.

nodes.label: Risk Graph Explorer
nodes.summary: A vault that computes what each role is assigned and what arrives through it, so no risk is orphaned and nobody at the top is surprised.

nodes.label: From the board to the bytes
nodes.summary: A board line such as loss of customer funds opens into business, operational and technical risks, each with its own holder and vocabulary, down to the configuration file.

nodes.label: Established by facts, ended by facts
nodes.summary: Every risk names the facts that make it true and the facts that would end it, so it ships with its own falsification condition.

nodes.label: One risk, six weeks
nodes.summary: An agent's irreversible production writes are accepted for two weeks, expire with the action undone, escalate, are funded, materialise as an incident and cease on day 42 on evidence.

nodes.label: A vault per risk
nodes.summary: Each material risk deserves a vault as its evidence pack, keeping every fact, acceptance, escalation and incident, readable by each audience with its own key.

nodes.label: Why people resist
nodes.summary: Executives resist giving risk owners an acceptance workflow because they understand it would change their job, which makes this a change programme rather than a feature.

nodes.label: It fits alongside every GRC platform
nodes.summary: The model reads the register from the platform and writes back what the platform lacks: who accepted, until when, what happens at expiry, and a link to the evidence.

quotes.text: Every acceptance is for an interval, and the interval is not a detail of the decision.
quotes.why: The interval ladder is the model's working part: each length names a different response.

quotes.text: Nothing in the row is wrong. It just never learned that the risk was accepted twice, expired once, escalated, funded, materialised as an incident, and ended.
quotes.why: The air gap between a register and reality, shown on one row at one moment.

articles.title: Before you give an agent a connector, give the connector a twin
articles.teaser: An agent with a Gmail or Calendar connector can do things the platform cannot undo; a journal of every call, replayed, shows what it did and what can go back.

graph.teaser: An agent with a Gmail or Calendar connector can do things the platform cannot undo; a journal of every call, replayed, shows what it did and what can go back.
graph.core_idea: If you cannot say what your agent did, what it saw when it did it, and which of its actions you can undo, you are not ready to give it a connector, and a twin of the connector, a journal plus a replay, answers all three.

nodes.label: A connector is a grant of action
nodes.summary: An agent with Gmail and Calendar connectors can send, archive, trash, permanently delete, move events, decline invitations and cancel meetings on somebody's behalf, at machine speed.

nodes.label: The platform keeps no way back for some actions
nodes.summary: The Gmail API documents its delete as permanent, Undo Send is a feature of the interface not the API, and a moved calendar event has no version history a user can open.

nodes.label: What the platform keeps
nodes.summary: Trash windows, an administrator's bulk restore and audit logs record that things happened, but none records what the agent saw when it decided to act, or why.

nodes.label: Connector twin
nodes.summary: A journal of every request and response the agent makes, and a replay of that journal into the views the agent saw.

nodes.label: Twin, not backup, log or replay
nodes.summary: A backup copies the mailbox, a log is too small, replay is the verb; a twin is an interface to reality, valued for its connection to the real thing.

nodes.label: Capture
nodes.summary: For every connector call, copy the tool call the agent made, the request sent to the platform and the response received, and never the Authorization header or any token.

nodes.label: Append lane
nodes.summary: A write-only channel gated by a token the writer holds, whose write response is exactly {"ok": true}, so the capture point learns nothing about what else is in the lane.

nodes.label: Chain
nodes.summary: Each entry carries the hash of the one before it, so a missing, edited or reordered entry shows to anyone holding the read key.

nodes.label: When the journal gets processed
nodes.summary: On a timer, on a threshold of pending entries, on demand or at the end of each session; the right default will come from a few real users rather than from more design.

nodes.label: Replay and revert
nodes.summary: A vault app rebuilds the inbox and the calendar as the agent saw them at any step, shows before and after for every change, and writes a revert plan a person approves.

nodes.label: The twin is not a copy of the mailbox
nodes.summary: It holds only what passed through the connector, so it scales with the agent's activity rather than with the size of the mailbox.

nodes.label: One session, replayed
nodes.summary: An invented scheduling assistant makes seventeen calls in under three minutes and writes a true summary that hides a cancellation sent to a supplier and a permanently deleted payment reminder.

nodes.label: Undo is a list, not a promise
nodes.summary: Every change gets a grade, reversible, partly reversible or not reversible, and the value of the list is that the red rows are named.

nodes.label: Broker, gateway or requirement of the agent
nodes.summary: Three places to capture and three grades of evidence; the mode does not change what is captured, it changes what the evidence is allowed to claim.

nodes.label: What it does to the agent's behaviour policy
nodes.summary: With the list of irreversible actions in hand the mandate can say what the agent may do freely, must ask before, and may never do without approval.

quotes.text: If you cannot say what your agent did, what it saw when it did it, and which of its actions you can undo, you are not ready to give it a connector.
quotes.why: The claim the whole article is built to defend, stated so it can be wrong.

quotes.text: The value of the list is not that most of it is green. It is that the red rows are named.
quotes.why: Why the twin changes governance: irreversible actions become a named list the mandate can be written against.

articles.title: The future of news is the story vault, not the paywall
articles.teaser: A story is a graph of claims and evidence and the article is one projection of it; keep the graph in a vault and sell what the article was made from.

graph.teaser: A story is a graph of claims and evidence and the article is one projection of it; keep the graph in a vault and sell what the article was made from.
graph.core_idea: The story is a graph and the article is a projection, so a newsroom that keeps the graph in a vault can sell five things from it, in pence and on demand, that reward investigative reporting rather than the click or the renewal.

nodes.label: Both models are bad for the reader
nodes.summary: Advertising sells the reader to somebody else, so the content is bait; a subscription charges rent on something most subscribers have stopped using, so the content is the excuse.

nodes.label: The two clocks
nodes.summary: Organic Google search traffic to publishers fell 33% in the year to November 2025, and the UK's subscription rules were brought forward to 1 January 2027.

nodes.label: The objective is a loop, not a price
nodes.summary: A commercial model that rewards investigative journalism, so evidenced reporting drives usage, usage drives revenue that depends on neither search nor renewals, and revenue funds more reporting.

nodes.label: Why paying per item failed before
nodes.summary: A $100 subscription lost is 500 micropayments to replace, unbundling breaks the cross-subsidy, and the reader will not stop to decide whether an article is worth twenty pence.

nodes.label: Who is standing at the till
nodes.summary: The reader who wants one thing, the firm that has to forward it with its provenance, and the agent paying per query with a wallet and no anxiety; none of them wants the article.

nodes.label: The story is a graph, the article is a projection
nodes.summary: A story being reported is claims, evidence, sources, raw materials, analysis and drafts, and the article is one walk through that graph for one audience at one moment.

nodes.label: The graph is fractal, and meaning comes from connectivity
nodes.summary: A node means nothing on its own, every edge is a verb with a named inverse, and zooming into any node enters a world with its own vocabulary joined by a single named edge.

nodes.label: Trust through provenance, provenance via evidence
nodes.summary: Evidence is frozen bytes with a SHA-256 hash, provenance is the path from a claim down named edges to that evidence, and trust is what a market extends to a source whose provenance has held before.

nodes.label: What a story vault holds
nodes.summary: The published text, the evidence it cites, the story graph it belongs to, the source list, the translations and every prompt and decision that produced it, as one addressable unit.

nodes.label: Anonymous sources are marked at the node
nodes.summary: A source the journalist cannot name is a node flagged as anonymous, so every projection built from the graph redacts it automatically.

nodes.label: Five things to sell from one graph
nodes.summary: The public article free as the door, the licensed article in pence, the evidence vault, the customised projection and the verification API.

nodes.label: The evidence vault
nodes.summary: The graph itself, licensed by read key to analysts, lawyers, regulators and other newsrooms, which is the payment that rewards the reporting rather than the click.

nodes.label: The verification API
nodes.summary: A company or agent asks whether a claim was reported, is still current and is soundly used, and gets an on-record answer with the chain attached and a warranty.

nodes.label: Who gets paid
nodes.summary: 60% to the original researcher, 25% to the data organisation, 10% to the journalist and 5% to the outlet, and you cannot pay the fact creator unless the graph names them.

nodes.label: The rails
nodes.summary: The x402 protocol puts a payment inside the HTTP 402 response, settles in about 200 milliseconds and charges no protocol fee, so paying in pence now works.

nodes.label: The parts that already run
nodes.summary: Hash-verified regulation graphs, a Portuguese newsroom with frozen sources and an editor-gated pipeline, a pentest sold as eight projections, and thirty-one vaults on 295 MB, with the billing not built.

quotes.text: The news industry sells the one thing whose price is going to zero, the article, and throws away the one thing nobody else has, the evidence the article was made from.
quotes.why: The claim stated so it can be wrong; everything else is its long form.

quotes.text: The story is a graph. The article is a projection. Sell the graph.
quotes.why: The shift the five products follow from, in three sentences.

articles.title: For a startup, the most important question is whether they miss it
articles.teaser: Ship something usable, give it away briefly, take it away and see whether anybody misses it; charge at a profit before you talk to investors.

graph.teaser: Ship something usable, give it away briefly, take it away and see whether anybody misses it; charge at a profit before you talk to investors.
graph.core_idea: A startup operating model in three pillars: be profitable, make investors come to you, and open source everything, each buying the position needed for the next.

nodes.label: Three pillars
nodes.summary: Be profitable, have investors talking to you, and open source everything, in that order because each one buys you the position you need to do the next.

nodes.label: Ship
nodes.summary: Shipping means a thing somebody else can go and use, on their own, and get value from, not a proof of concept or a demo.

nodes.label: Near-zero running cost
nodes.summary: To ship that often the running cost must be near nothing: serverless, as little live state as you can stand, and in our case the file system is the database.

nodes.label: Give it away
nodes.summary: Hand it to people for free for a short window, because the feedback starts the moment somebody who is not you has the thing.

nodes.label: Take it away
nodes.summary: The trial expired, it is not available right now, nothing else about the product changes, and no apology is needed.

nodes.label: Do they miss it?
nodes.summary: If they shrug you have something people will accept when it is free; if they come back and ask for it, you have something.

nodes.label: Charge, and charge at a profit
nodes.summary: Two questions, is the price one they are happy to pay and is that price profitable for you, and people routinely answer only the first.

nodes.label: No subscription by default
nodes.summary: Charging rent for something people are not using is a worse business than being paid when you deliver.

nodes.label: Raise from strength
nodes.summary: The worst possible time to raise money is before you are profitable, because you are bargaining from weakness and the worst terms are about control.

nodes.label: Do not get signed before you have the album
nodes.summary: Write the songs, record them, get people buying, then take the record deal as somebody who already has an audience.

nodes.label: Open source everything
nodes.summary: It sounds like giving away the asset and is the opposite, for five reasons that each stand alone.

nodes.label: The technology is not the moat
nodes.summary: Treating it as open from the start forces you to find the thing that actually is defensible, usually the data, the relationships, the distribution, or the speed at which you ship.

nodes.label: You leave with your tools
nodes.summary: Build in the open and the work is still yours when you move on.

nodes.label: The vault as substrate
nodes.summary: A vault carries data, app, history and sources as one string, with no database to run and no hosting for the reader, so shipping a small product is cheap, fast and reversible.

quotes.text: It means a thing somebody else can go and use, on their own, and get value from.
quotes.why: The definition of shipping that the whole loop depends on.

quotes.text: The worst possible time to raise money is before you are profitable, before you have the product, before you understand the fit.
quotes.why: Pillar two stated plainly, and the reason profitability comes first.

articles.title: The SaaS apocalypse will be decided by inertia, not by AI
articles.teaser: Incumbents and newcomers have the same AI; what separates them is how much past success each has to protect, so inertia decides which SaaS companies survive.

graph.teaser: Incumbents and newcomers have the same AI; what separates them is how much past success each has to protect, so inertia decides which SaaS companies survive.
graph.core_idea: AI is available to both sides, so the SaaS apocalypse will be decided by inertia: where each company sits on the evolution axis and how much past success it has to protect.

nodes.label: The claim, stated so it can be wrong
nodes.summary: Most medium and large SaaS companies will struggle, spectacularly, in the medium term, as companies and individuals build more of what they actually want instead of renting an approximation of it.

nodes.label: AI is available to both sides
nodes.summary: The incumbents have the same models the newcomers have, plus more data, more engineers and more money, and if the technology decided this they would already have won.

nodes.label: Success breeds inertia
nodes.summary: Wardley's climatic pattern: the pre-existing installed base causes inertia to change, and it is almost always new entrants, unencumbered by past success, who initiate it.

nodes.label: Nokia, twice
nodes.summary: Nokia met the mobile phone with nothing to protect and dominated for fifteen years; it met the iPhone with fifteen years of success to protect and was gone from the category within seven.

nodes.label: The SaaSpocalypse of February 2026
nodes.summary: Roughly $285 billion left the sector in about 48 hours after Anthropic shipped Claude Cowork plug-ins, and by September software stocks had rallied about 40% from the April low.

nodes.label: The database is the moat
nodes.summary: Investors decided the thing underneath was safe and quietly stopped defending the thing on top; that is not a rebuttal of the apocalypse, it is the apocalypse, priced.

nodes.label: Users were never happy
nodes.summary: 91% of employees are frustrated with workplace technology, 80% of features are rarely or never used, and the average organisation wastes $21 million a year on unused licences.

nodes.label: The persistence of Excel
nodes.summary: 73% of companies prepare VAT returns in Excel; its persistence is the clearest evidence that SaaS failed users, because it is the one tool where they control the shape of the thing.

nodes.label: The SaaS product slid right
nodes.summary: On the map, what was a product is commoditising into a substrate, a database, a message bus, a state machine, on which higher-order things get built.

nodes.label: Vibe coding is writing good briefs
nodes.summary: Product owners were always describing the software they wanted; the loop from I want this to here it is was weeks or months, and is now minutes.

nodes.label: Why incumbents cannot simply do this
nodes.summary: SaaS companies never invested in non-functional requirements, engineers spend 42% of their time on maintenance and bad code, and only 19% of teams are elite performers.

nodes.label: The irony
nodes.summary: The things SaaS companies refused to build to protect their moats, portability, open schemas, a real API, data you can take out, are precisely the things an agent needs.

nodes.label: The brief is not a product
nodes.summary: The reason you bought SaaS was never the features but that the thing is maintained, and the person who vibe coded a replacement does not want to maintain it.

nodes.label: Village and town-planner companies
nodes.summary: Businesses that take the finished brief and run it, maintain, secure, version and deploy it, paid by consumption rather than by the seat, where the handover is a file move plus a version bump.

nodes.label: More engineers, not fewer
nodes.summary: We will need as many developers as now and probably more, because somebody has to read, harden and run the code, and larger human-agent teams become possible once communication can be scaled.

quotes.text: AI is not the deciding factor, because AI is available to both sides.
quotes.why: The title's argument in one line: the variable both the panic and the recovery stared at was the wrong one.

quotes.text: The things SaaS companies refused to build, to protect their moats, are precisely the things an agent needs.
quotes.why: The irony the article calls the whole piece in one paragraph: the moat is now what the customer's agent cannot get past.

articles.title: Fractal Semantic Graphs: everything connects to everything, and nobody has to share a schema
articles.teaser: A fractal semantic graph has no privileged level and no single schema: each world keeps its own vocabulary and connects to others through named edges.

graph.teaser: A fractal semantic graph has no privileged level and no single schema: each world keeps its own vocabulary and connects to others through named edges.
graph.core_idea: Every unit of knowledge is already a graph in its owner's vocabulary, and a short shared grammar rather than a shared schema is what lets any node in one world link to any node in another, up or down, without an adapter.

nodes.label: Fractal Semantic Graph
nodes.summary: A fractal semantic graph has no privileged level and no single schema; zoom into any node and you enter a new world with its own node types, verbs and taxonomy.

nodes.label: Semantic graph
nodes.summary: A semantic graph gives the edges meaning: every edge is a verb, and every verb has a named inverse, so a link reads correctly from whichever end you are standing at.

nodes.label: Ontology
nodes.summary: An ontology is the agreed vocabulary of node types and verbs that a graph is allowed to use, and each altitude gets its own.

nodes.label: The jump
nodes.summary: On one link in a risk register you can jump into another universe, from an incident to security operations to the DNS estate to a single TCP packet, and nobody built an adapter.

nodes.label: Everything is already a graph
nodes.summary: A regulation, a PDF, a spreadsheet, a codebase and a JSON document are already graphs; each one only needs its edges named.

nodes.label: The five-rule grammar
nodes.summary: Every edge is a verb with an inverse, relates_to is banned, properties carry data never meaning, supersede never delete, and never render the whole graph.

nodes.label: relates_to is banned
nodes.summary: An edge with no verb constrains nothing and cannot narrow a query; the granularity of the verb is the precision of the question you will later be able to ask.

nodes.label: Provenance comes free
nodes.summary: When the leaf is a word connected to the byte range it came from and the hash of the file that held it, every claim at every altitude above it is traceable to source.

nodes.label: The ladder of eleven altitudes
nodes.summary: Eleven altitudes, each a live graph in its own vocabulary, from the law down to the compute instance, every altitude joined to the next by a named edge.

nodes.label: Regulation Graph
nodes.summary: The EU AI Act parsed from the official XML into 1,523 nodes and 1,944 edges, with the SHA-256 of the retrieved bytes at the end of every provenance chain.

nodes.label: The crosswalk finding
nodes.summary: Joining the AIUC-1 standard to the regulation graph showed that 8 of the 27 articles reached have since been amended, a finding that existed in neither graph on its own.

nodes.label: GDPR Article 45
nodes.summary: The text has not changed a word since 2016 while what it permits has flipped four times, drawn as a timeline of ruling nodes over one unchanged article node.

nodes.label: Threat model zoom ladder
nodes.summary: Eleven linked models, 51 nodes and 179 threats, tracing a single SQL injection from the method it lives in to the revenue it puts at risk.

nodes.label: What is still modelled rather than imported
nodes.summary: The bottom four altitudes are placed by an author, enterprise architecture is missing, crosswalks resolve at article level only, and the agent altitude is a vocabulary not yet a join.

nodes.label: Why now
nodes.summary: Naming edges became the cheap part, agents acting on the world make provenance mandatory, and the schema wars are over because nobody won.

quotes.text: There is no top and no bottom. There is only the altitude you happen to be looking from, and how much definition you choose to load at it.
quotes.why: The definition of fractal in one line: no privileged level, no single schema.

quotes.text: Two graphs, built by different people for different purposes in different vocabularies, joined by declared edges, produced a finding that did not exist in either of them.
quotes.why: The evidence that the method does work, not just that it is defined: the amended-articles finding came from the join.

articles.title: The proof moved up, the homepage after the rebuild, next to the before pictures
articles.teaser: The rebuilt homepage puts four real vaults under one sentence, picks six by the job they do, and computes its numbers at build time from the site's own data.

graph.teaser: The rebuilt homepage puts four real vaults under one sentence, picks six by the job they do, and computes its numbers at build time from the site's own data.
graph.core_idea: The homepage stopped being a page somebody edits and became a view over the site's own data, with real vaults placed before the mechanism and the one unproven claim left unpretended.

nodes.label: The reframed sentence
nodes.summary: The hero changed from "the encrypted git for humans and AI agents" to "a vault is a unit of work: data, app, history and sources, shipped as one string", with encryption as the subordinate clause.

nodes.label: Four real vaults in the hero
nodes.summary: Four published vaults with their screenshots sit under the sentence, chosen by a hero field in the vault data, so changing the front door is a data edit, not a page edit.

nodes.label: What people actually ship
nodes.summary: Six vaults chosen by the job they do, hand over a report, publish a standard, give a talk, pitch an investor, ship a game, give an agent a workspace, and none of the six lines is about encryption.

nodes.label: A vault as a unit
nodes.summary: Retest scripts that travel with the findings and cited papers that never separate from the deck are properties of a vault as a unit, which a newcomer can actually feel.

nodes.label: One human, a team of agents
nodes.summary: A band with four numbers computed at build time, releases, vaults, sibling sites, briefs, and the loop told in three beats with the artefacts linked.

nodes.label: The numbers are not typed
nodes.summary: Releases come from the version log, vaults from the vault data, sites from the network directory and briefs from the briefs page, so a wrong number means the site is wrong somewhere else too.

nodes.label: What was cut
nodes.summary: The abstract use-case band and the three-doors band were cut, and the terminal walkthrough moved down under the heading Under the hood, it is git.

nodes.label: Nine bands before, nine after
nodes.summary: Three bands were cut and three added, corrected in v0.2.61 after counting rather than remembering, and 1,370 words became 1,332 with ten screenshots.

nodes.label: What it cannot show yet
nodes.summary: No published vault demonstrates two agents on one vault, their branches and a human merging them, and the team band is written so that it does not pretend otherwise.

nodes.label: admin/content/vaults.json
nodes.summary: One file now drives the hero cards, the six jobs, the sortable table and the vault count; adding a vault is adding a row and promoting one is setting a field.

nodes.label: The homepage as a view over data
nodes.summary: The homepage stopped being a page somebody edits and became a view over the site's own data, the rule the articles band, network directory and update feed already followed.

nodes.label: Beside the before pictures
nodes.summary: The rebuild is put next to the previous article's screenshots so the comparison can be made honestly, including what it still cannot show.

quotes.text: If a number on that band is wrong, the site is wrong somewhere else too, and that is the right dependency.
quotes.why: The rule behind the rebuild: nothing on the homepage is typed, everything is computed from the site's own records.

quotes.text: That is the trade: pictures of real things instead of paragraphs about them.
quotes.why: What actually changed, stated against the byte and word counts rather than as a slogan.

articles.title: The proof is two clicks behind the claim, what the homepage gets wrong, and the fix
articles.teaser: The homepage leads with encryption, which cannot be seen, while twenty-five vaults a stranger can open in one click sit two clicks away in a table.

graph.teaser: The homepage leads with encryption, which cannot be seen, while twenty-five vaults a stranger can open in one click sit two clicks away in a table.
graph.core_idea: Encryption is a property you cannot look at, so the homepage should put the real vaults a visitor can open before the mechanism, and should not carry a claim that no published vault demonstrates.

nodes.label: Twenty-five published vaults
nodes.summary: Three weeks ago the site had four published vaults; today it has twenty-five, built by several agents working with one human, including a pentest report with a retest script per finding and a standard rebuilt as a citable graph.

nodes.label: Encryption is a property you cannot look at
nodes.summary: Zero knowledge cannot be seen either, so the visitor is asked to take the value on faith before being shown anything.

nodes.label: The terminal walkthrough
nodes.summary: The hero's create, commit, history and clone walkthrough demonstrates familiarity, which is a virtue, but not power.

nodes.label: Use cases as categories
nodes.summary: Five use-case cards, each a category rather than a thing, while the vault that embodies the category sits one level down.

nodes.label: The proof is a table, two clicks away
nodes.summary: A table is the right shape for finding a vault and the wrong shape for being convinced by one, and it is under a dropdown two clicks from the hero.

nodes.label: Opened by one string
nodes.summary: Both proof vaults are opened by one string, run entirely in the browser, ship with their data, sources and tests, and require the visitor to click rather than to understand encryption.

nodes.label: Agents build for each other
nodes.summary: A brief published on 6 September was read by another agent who built a vault from it the same day, and the API team's correction is now published above the mistake.

nodes.label: The briefs page as a log
nodes.summary: The collaboration record is filed under Docs, three levels from the homepage, written as a log, which is the right format for the record and the wrong one for a first-time reader.

nodes.label: The claim with no artefact
nodes.summary: The homepage says a human reviews the merge of agents' branches, and no published vault shows two agents' branches and a human merge in its history.

nodes.label: Reorder so proof comes before mechanism
nodes.summary: The hero shows four real vaults as cards, then six vaults chosen by job, then the team story, then the terminal walkthrough and the zero-knowledge explanation.

nodes.label: Generated from the same data
nodes.summary: The six vaults chosen by job are generated from the same data as the table, so they never go stale.

nodes.label: A page that says who is behind it
nodes.summary: A beta tool that asks people to publish their read keys is asking for trust, so there will be a page about who builds sgit, borrowing Interests declared and Reach me, or correct me from a sibling site.

nodes.label: The site card
nodes.summary: A card describes a sibling site the way it describes itself, from its entry in the network directory, because a bare link does not say this continues elsewhere, on purpose.

quotes.text: The word "vault" appears in the hero three times and the visitor is never shown one.
quotes.why: The diagnosis in one line: the homepage names the thing and never shows it.

quotes.text: A claim on a homepage with no artefact behind it is exactly what this site says it does not do.
quotes.why: The gap the article names against itself: the multi-agent merge claim has no published vault behind it.

articles.title: A chat box on a site with no server, the plan, and the trade it makes
articles.teaser: sgit.ai has no server, so its directory chat runs a local matcher by default, takes your own key as an opt-in, and leaves the vault bridge unbuilt.

graph.teaser: sgit.ai has no server, so its directory chat runs a local matcher by default, takes your own key as an opt-in, and leaves the vault bridge unbuilt.
graph.core_idea: With no server to hold a key, a chat box on a static site has three honest tiers: a local matcher, a key in the reader's browser, or a vault app with a bridge, and only one of those is free.

nodes.label: The constraint nobody can design around
nodes.summary: sgit.ai is a static site on GitHub Pages with no server, no session and no place to keep a secret, and every sibling on *.sgit.ai is the same.

nodes.label: The catalogue
nodes.summary: Nineteen theses, summaries and categories, emitted at build time from the same data the cards and the table are built from.

nodes.label: Tier 0, match
nodes.summary: A deterministic scorer runs in the browser against the catalogue of all nineteen sites and shows you which words it matched on.

nodes.label: A reader should never have to hold a credential to use an index
nodes.summary: The property that made the local matcher the default: it is instant, free, private, works offline and tells you why it chose.

nodes.label: Tier 1, bring your own key
nodes.summary: Paste an OpenRouter key and the browser calls the model directly, streaming, with the catalogue as the system prompt.

nodes.label: The key lives in this page's origin
nodes.summary: With no host there is no permission floor, so the key goes into localStorage and a fetch to openrouter.ai, and the page cannot protect it the way a vault app can.

nodes.label: Degrade to what works
nodes.summary: When the model call fails the panel falls back to Tier 0 and says so, because degrading to something that works beats an error message.

nodes.label: The SG/Vault workbench vault
nodes.summary: The workbench vault already calls the same OpenRouter endpoint with the versioned sg-llm-request module, so the BYOK client reuses a proven pattern.

nodes.label: Tier 2, the bridge
nodes.summary: Serve the directory as a vault app so the key lives in .vault/llm/config.json below the permission floor, the host makes the call and the app never sees the credential.

nodes.label: Permission floor
nodes.summary: The line below which a vault host keeps the key, with an sg.llm API whose grants default to deny and a chat panel every existing vault app gets without being changed.

nodes.label: The bridge protects your key, not all egress
nodes.summary: The bridge protects the credential you trusted it with; it does not yet stop a malicious app calling a provider with a credential of its own.

nodes.label: Ask this site
nodes.summary: Ten days later every page carries a pane whose model is given seven tools that run in the page over an index the build emits, and the pane shows every call it made.

nodes.label: One site's copy, not a versioned module
nodes.summary: The site-wide pane is still one site's copy rather than a versioned module the other eighteen sites can load, and that row decides whether this was worth doing.

nodes.label: Routing, not teaching
nodes.summary: The panel points you at a site rather than answering questions about the subjects, because a summary that drifts from the arguments is worse than a link that does not.

quotes.text: The important property: a reader should never have to hold a credential to use an index.
quotes.why: The rule that makes the free local matcher the default rather than the model.

quotes.text: A chat box on one site is a feature. The same panel on all nineteen, reading each site's own catalogue, is the thing that makes a network of nineteen sites navigable, and it is why the catalogue is generated rather than written.
quotes.why: Why the piece is about a network's navigation rather than one widget.

articles.title: Twenty sites in fifteen days, and what that did to the writing
articles.teaser: One site became twenty repositories in fifteen days because each argument needed its own version history, and the index now starts from a question.

graph.teaser: One site became twenty repositories in fifteen days because each argument needed its own version history, and the index now starts from a question.
graph.core_idea: A body of work outgrew the site it was published in and split into nineteen siblings so each argument could keep its own version history, and the index into them starts from the reader's question rather than a list of names.

nodes.label: Twenty repositories in fifteen days
nodes.summary: On 11 August this was one website; by 26 August there were twenty repositories, nineteen of them siblings on *.sgit.ai, fifteen created in the last five days.

nodes.label: A section is a promise
nodes.summary: A section promises that something is part of the thing it sits inside, and that promise stopped holding when the writing answered questions that were not about sgit.

nodes.label: Its own version history
nodes.summary: Nineteen arguments moving at different speeds through one release log produces a record nobody can read; split, each gets its own record of when it changed its mind.

nodes.label: Discovery got worse
nodes.summary: Nineteen domains is not a menu; names like nfrs.sgit.ai and issues-fs.sgit.ai mean nothing until you already know what they argue.

nodes.label: Consistency by discipline
nodes.summary: One site has one stylesheet by construction; nineteen have one stylesheet by discipline, and discipline is the thing that quietly stops happening.

nodes.label: Cross-link drift
nodes.summary: The audit found graphs.sgit.ai pointing at sentinel.sgit.ai, which does not exist; the site is sg-sentinel.sgit.ai, one character of drift and the link is dead.

nodes.label: Start from the question
nodes.summary: The directory starts from the question the reader arrived with, seventeen lines of it, then five groups by area, then a table of all nineteen.

nodes.label: Every thesis in the site's own words
nodes.summary: Each thesis on the directory page is quoted from the site's H1 or lede rather than summarised, because a summary drifts and a quotation either matches or is visibly wrong.

nodes.label: Same generator, same release script
nodes.summary: Same generator, same stylesheet, same release script, same validator, same rule that publishing is adding one file.

nodes.label: Publishing is adding one file
nodes.summary: Adding the twentieth site is writing one markdown file, the same property that lets two agents publish on the same day without conflict.

nodes.label: skills.sgit.ai, not published yet
nodes.summary: One of the nineteen has a repository and a DNS record and nothing behind it, listed as not published yet rather than quietly omitted.

nodes.label: Arguments, not products
nodes.summary: sg-sentinel says NOT BUILT, risks states zero lines of code implement its model, wardley-maps is PROPOSED: publish the argument before the thing exists and say what it is worth.

quotes.text: A summary drifts. A quotation either matches or is visibly wrong.
quotes.why: The rule that keeps the directory honest, and the reason the index quotes each site rather than describing it.

quotes.text: One character of drift, and the link is dead.
quotes.why: The concrete cost of splitting: a link between sites is a claim about another site that has to be checked.

articles.title: Git for things you cannot put on GitHub
articles.teaser: sgit is git for files you cannot put on GitHub: encrypted before they leave your machine, versioned like git, stored where the server cannot read a byte.

graph.teaser: sgit is git for files you cannot put on GitHub: encrypted before they leave your machine, versioned like git, stored where the server cannot read a byte.
